newsitem.title: BOSNIA: Ousted Serb officers snub civilian marching orders.
newsitem.headline: Ousted Serb officers snub civilian marching orders.

text.p: Senior Bosnian Serb commanders on Monday snubbed new military leaders installed by civilian authorities this weekend, calling them lightweight party hacks and vowing disobedience.

President Biljana Plavsic swore in a new commander of the Bosnian Serb army after dismissing General Ratko Mladic and senior commanders who fought beside him in the 1992-95 separatist war with Moslems and Croats.
Mladic, indicted for war crimes by the United Nations and reported to be ailing, kept a low profile but sources at his headquarters said he retained the army's loyalty.
A group of about 100 high-ranking officers in the Bosnian Serb army said in Banja Luka on Monday they backed their sacked commander and expressed "disgust" at the dismissals.

The officers express "full support for the (army) main headquarters led by General Mladic, as they are the only ones to guarantee the survival of the Serb Republic," said a statement faxed to Reuters.
The officers dismissed the newly appointed army commander and his deputy as lightweight party hacks without proper military schooling or combat experience.
The statement said new army chief Major-General Pero Colic had called a meeting of military commanders, but it failed to go ahead after none turned up.
"The officers who refused to attend the meeting... simply could not accept to betray their wartime commanders in the central staff and corps, who have proved their patriotism."
But the Bosnian Serb news agency SRNA later on Monday said Colic had met corps commanders earlier in the day and indicated a compromise might have been reached.
SRNA is under tight control by the civilian authorities and its report, just like the statement by the 100 officers, could not be independently confirmed.

"The commanders of all corps fully accepted all decisions of the Supreme Defence Council on the establishment of the General Staff, as well as other decisions on the reorganization and consolidation of the army," SRNA said.
"A number of officers were appointed to new posts or relieved of duties. Most of those relieved of duty will remain in the BSA, while a small number will be retired," it said.
But the biggest opponents of the Pale authorities, Generals Milan Gvero and Grujo Boric and Colonel Milovan Milutinovic, did not survive the purge.

SRNA said General Zdravko Tolimir, the powerful Bosnian Serb army security chief and close aide of Mladic, would be retired but could be later offered the post of "presidential adviser for the military implementation of the Dayton agreement".
SRNA said the chief of the powerful Krajina corps based in Banja Luka, General Momir Talic, would keep his post.
Mladic, a hero among Bosnian Serbs, survived a similar attempt to sack him last year, but the army has been weakened since peace was restored and the civilian police has grown in influence.
NATO peacekeepers and international mediators are watching the internal power struggle nervously, hoping it will not derail the precarious peace process in Bosnia.
Sources close to Mladic told Reuters the standoff would not be violent but would "last a long time".
Diplomats suspected Serbian President Slobodan Milosevic was behind the purge for domestic and foreign policy reasons.
Milosevic, the guarantor of Bosnian Serb compliance with the Dayton peace agreement, needs to reassure the West in order to get the remaining sanctions against Yugoslavia lifted.
He acted similarly in 1992 when he axed scores of generals after withdrawing the old Yugoslav Federal Army (JNA) from secessionist wars in Croatia and Bosnia.
Just hours before Mladic's dismissal was made public, the Belgrade newspaper Politika, close to Milosevic, issued a rare rebuke on Friday to the Bosnian Serb army for interfering in civilian affairs.
